messages.subject: "Transdimensional" Model Comparison
parts:
Hi All,

Following a JAGS example on John Kruschke's blog, I am trying to do a model comparison to obtain p(M1|D) / p(M2|D), for a simple model and a more sophisticated model.

In his examples, he often samples from dcat:

modelIndex ~ dcat( modelProbability[] )

where I take modelProbability to be a vector of {0.5,0.5} and so modelIndex "emits" 1 or 2.  Then, I can use an expression like:

a[g] <- mu[g] * kappa[g] * (modelIndex - 1) + mu0 * kappa0 * (2-modelIndex)

and a similar expression for b[g].

My questions:
1) when I try my Stan incarnation (please see attached files for code and sample data), modelIndex which I model in a similar way is zero!  Hence, the trick won't work.  Is there a proper Stan idiom?

2) If I were able to pull this off, how would I "aggregate" the values of modelIndex so that I can take the ratio of 1's and 2's to get the ratio that I seek?  It seems that parameters may only be real, and I haven't figured out how to cast the integer modelIndex into a real-declared variable due to what appears to be visibility/scope.

Thanks,
Eric

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: "Transdimensional" Model Comparison
parts:
Stan does not yet support sampling of discrete parameters that have parents with other parameters. See sections 1.3 and 9.1 of the manual, for some discussion. 

So the Metropolis-Hastings-Green trick I think you are attempting just won't work yet in Stan. Likewise, it's not possible to do imputation or measurement error on discrete data types.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: marginalizing discrete params for model comparison (was Re: "Transdimensional" Model Comparison)
parts:
On 11/24/12 2:26 PM, Richard McElreath wrote:
> Stan does not yet support sampling of discrete parameters that have parents with other parameters.

Stan doesn't yet support any discrete sampling. When we
add random number generating functions, we'll be able to forward-sample
discrete variables (sample when all parents are known and no children).

We will add discrete sampling over the next half a year or so.
It's a big job, but I think we're mostly there in terms of a
full design and the outline of an implementation.

For now, many of these models can have their discrete
parameters marginalized out, including Eric Brown's original
example that spawned this thread. The relevant parts of the
original (buggy) definition are as follows.

data {
vector<2> modelProb;
...
model {

int modelIndex; // declared, but not defined!
...
modelIndex ~ categorical(modelProb); // still not defined
...
a[g] <- ( mu[g] *kappa[g])*(modelIndex-1) + a0*(2-modelIndex);
b[g] <- ((1.0-mu[g])*kappa[g])*(modelIndex-1) + b0*(2-modelIndex);
...
for( i in 1:nIndividuals )
theta[i] ~ beta(a[ groupIndex[i] ], b[ groupIndex[i] ]);

for( i in 1:nIndividuals )
y[i] ~ binomial( N[i], theta[i] );

The problem is that the modelIndex here is a local variable
and it's not defined when you get to the modelIndex ~ ... statement.
The sampling statement

modelIndex ~ categorical(modelProb); // still not defined

in the model is equivalent in Stan to writing this:

lp__ <- lp__ + categorical_log(modelIndex,modelProb);

That is, it doesn't do random number generation where it is executed,
it just adds to the log probability function return accumulator lp__.

For beta-binomial structures like yours:

for( i in 1:nIndividuals )
theta[i] ~ beta(a[ groupIndex[i] ], b[ groupIndex[i] ]);

for( i in 1:nIndividuals )
y[i] ~ binomial( N[i], theta[i] );

You can marginalize out theta[i] by using:

for (i in 1:nIndividuals)
y[i] ~ beta_binomial(n[i], a[groupIndex[i]], b[groupIndex[i]]);

This should be more efficient both in execution speed and
in mixing (though I haven't tried it and the geometric
implications of some of these moves continues to surprise me).
And it clears the way for marginalizing out modelIndex as follows:

for (i in 1:2)
a[g,i] <- mu[g] * kappa[g]) * (model_idx - 1)
+ a0 * (2 - model_idx);
b[g,i] <- (1.0 - mu[g]) * kappa[g]* (model_idx - 1)
+ b0 * (2 - model_idx);
}

Then you can marginalize out the indexes contribution as
follows (the log_sum_exp is just for arithmetical stability --
see the manual section on marginalizing out discrete params
for simpler examples):

for (i in 1:nIndivudals) {
int g;
g <- groupIndex[i];
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(modelProb[1]) + beta_binomial_log(y[i],a[g,1],b[g,1]),
log(modelProb[2]) + beta_binomial_log(y[i],a[g,2],b[g,2]));
}

That clears the way algebraically for a further simplification:

a1[g] <- mu[g] *kappa[g];
b1[g] <- (1.0-mu[g]) * kappa[g];
...
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(modelProb[1]) + beta_binomial_log(y[i],a1[g],b1[g]),
log(modelProb[2]) + beta_binomial_log(y[i],a0,b0)));

---------------------------

I don't know much about model comparison, but if you make modelProb
a bounded scalar parameter defined as:

real<lower=0,upper=1> model1Prob;

and take model2Prob = 1 - model1Prob, you could fit the mixture
rather than defining it as data.

-------------------------

Also, in the model, I saw the following:

mMu ~ uniform(0.,1.);
kMu ~ gamma(1.,1/0.1);
aMu <- fmax( 0.01, mMu * kMu);
bMu <- fmax( 0.01, (1.0 - mMu) * kMu);

for( g in 1:nGroups ) {
mu[g] ~ beta( aMu, bMu ) ;

This is dangerous. If mMu * kMu < 0.01, you lose the connection to
the gradient altogether and Stan is unlikely to recover.

I'd try it without these constraints first, and then if there are
arithmetic precision issues, constrain the parameters in both their declarations
and their definitions to achieve the effect you want.

- Bob
